cards.explanation: The answer is faithful. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus, writes that Jesus "…considered me faithful and appointed me to service." Look at who is doing the considering: Jesus, not Paul. Paul isn't bragging about his résumé here, friends. He's saying thank you, and I'd be thanking Him too.

The answer is mercy. Paul says it plainly: "…I was shown mercy." Blasphemer, persecutor, violent man, and still mercy. That's the whole point of the verse, friends. Mercy shows up right where you'd least expect it.

The answer is True. Paul says he "…had acted in ignorance and unbelief…" Then he adds that he was shown mercy. He's not making excuses for the blasphemy, the persecuting and the violence. He's just telling us how it was, and that mercy found him anyway.

The answer is faith and love. Paul says the grace of our Lord overflowed to him, "…along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus." Grace didn't show up by itself, friends. It brought faith and love with it. That's some serious gift wrapping.
The answer is that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. Paul calls this saying trustworthy and worthy of full acceptance. That's the saying, friends, short and sweet.

The answer is worst. Paul says Christ Jesus came to save sinners, "…of whom I am the worst." He doesn't dodge it or soften it. Then in the next verse he tells us why mercy found him. If the worst can be saved, bakers, nobody's too far gone.

The answer is so Jesus could display His patience as an example. Paul writes that he was shown mercy "…so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life." So Paul himself is the example. If Jesus can be that patient with him, there's hope for everybody who comes after.
The answer is False. Paul writes that Christ Jesus displayed "…His perfect patience…" That's not a little, friends, and it's not just enough to get by. It's complete. Paul is the example of it.

The answer is eternal life. Paul says Jesus' patience with him is "…an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life." Eternal life is what those believers are trusting Him for. If He was that patient with Paul, He can be patient with whoever believes in Him.

The answer is False. Paul calls Him "…the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God…" Eternal and immortal mean this King doesn't pass away. And Paul says honor and glory belong to Him "…forever and ever." Amen!

The answer is fight the good fight. Paul writes to Timothy, whom he calls his child, that the command is "…in keeping with the previous prophecies about you, so that by them you may fight the good fight…" So the prophecies are there to help him in that fight. That's some real backup, friends.

The answer is by holding on to faith and a good conscience. Paul tells Timothy to fight the good fight "…holding on to faith and a good conscience…" So the way to fight is to hold on. I'll take a firm grip any day, bakers, especially when the dough gets slippery.

The answer is shipwrecked. Paul tells Timothy to hold on to faith and a good conscience, "…which some have rejected and thereby shipwrecked their faith." A shipwreck is a hard picture, friends. That's the word he uses, and it's a heavy one.

The answer is Hymenaeus and Alexander. Paul names them: "Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander…" They're among those who shipwrecked their faith. Paul says he has handed them over to Satan "…to be taught not to blaspheme."

The answer is True. Paul writes that he has "…handed over to Satan…" Hymenaeus and Alexander "…to be taught not to blaspheme." The aim he states is that they be taught. This is a heavy part of the letter, friends, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.
